I read a sci-fi short story called "The Egg" By Andy Weir and it took me on a mind trip.

You were on your way home when you died. It was a car accident. Nothing particularly remarkable, but fatal nonetheless. You left behind a wife and two children. It was a painless death. The EMTs tried their best to save you, but to no avail. Your body was so utterly shattered you were better off, trust me. And that’s when you met me. “What… what happened?” You asked. “Where am I?” “You died,” I said, matter-of-factly. No point in mincing words. “There was a… a truck and it was skidding…” “Yup,” I said. “I… I died?” “Yup. But don’t feel bad about it. Everyone dies,” I said. You looked around. There was nothingness. Just you and me. “What is this place?” You asked. “Is this the afterlife?” “More or less,” I said. “Are you god?” You asked. “Yup,” I replied. “I’m God.” “My kids… my wife,” you said. “What about them?” “Will they be all right?” “That’s what I like to see,” I said. “You just died and your main concern is for your family. That’s good stuff right there.” You looked at me with fascination. To you, I didn’t look like God. I just looked like some man. Or possibly a woman. Some vague authority figure, maybe. More of a grammar school teacher than the almighty. “Don’t worry,” I said. “They’ll be fine. Your kids will remember you as perfect in every way. They didn’t have time to grow contempt for you. Your wife will cry on the outside, but will be secretly relieved. To be fair, your marriage was falling apart. If it’s any consolation, she’ll feel very guilty for feeling relieved.” “Oh,” you said. “So what happens now? Do I go to heaven or hell or something?” “Neither,” I said. “You’ll be reincarnated.” “Ah,” you said. “So the Hindus were right,” “All religions are right in their own way,” I said. “Walk with me.” You followed along as we strode through the void. “Where are we going?” “Nowhere in particular,” I said. “It’s just nice to walk while we talk.” “So what’s the point, then?” You asked. “When I get reborn, I’ll just be a blank slate, right? A baby. So all my experiences and everything I did in this life won’t matter.” “Not so!” I said. “You have within you all the knowledge and experiences of all your past lives. You just don’t remember them right now.” I stopped walking and took you by the shoulders. “Your soul is more magnificent, beautiful, and gigantic than you can possibly imagine. A human mind can only contain a tiny fraction of what you are. It’s like sticking your finger in a glass of water to see if it’s hot or cold. You put a tiny part of yourself into the vessel, and when you bring it back out, you’ve gained all the experiences it had. “You’ve been in a human for the last 48 years, so you haven’t stretched out yet and felt the rest of your immense consciousness. If we hung out here for long enough, you’d start remembering everything. But there’s no point to doing that between each life.” “How many times have I been reincarnated, then?” “Oh lots. Lots and lots. An in to lots of different lives.” I said. “This time around, you’ll be a Chinese peasant girl in 540 AD.” “Wait, what?” You stammered. “You’re sending me back in time?” “Well, I guess technically. Time, as you know it, only exists in your universe. Things are different where I come from.” “Where you come from?” You said. “Oh sure,” I explained “I come from somewhere. Somewhere else. And there are others like me. I know you’ll want to know what it’s like there, but honestly you wouldn’t understand.” “Oh,” you said, a little let down. “But wait. If I get reincarnated to other places in time, I could have interacted with myself at some point.” “Sure. Happens all the time. And with both lives only aware of their own lifespan you don’t even know it’s happening.” “So what’s the point of it all?” “Seriously?” I asked. “Seriously? You’re asking me for the meaning of life? Isn’t that a little stereotypical?” “Well it’s a reasonable question,” you persisted. I looked you in the eye. “The meaning of life, the reason I made this whole universe, is for you to mature.” “You mean mankind? You want us to mature?” “No, just you. I made this whole universe for you. With each new life you grow and mature and become a larger and greater intellect.” “Just me? What about everyone else?” “There is no one else,” I said. “In this universe, there’s just you and me.” You stared blankly at me. “But all the people on earth…” “All you. Different incarnations of you.” “Wait. I’m everyone!?” “Now you’re getting it,” I said, with a congratulatory slap on the back. “I’m every human being who ever lived?” “Or who will ever live, yes.” “I’m Abraham Lincoln?” “And you’re John Wilkes Booth, too,” I added. “I’m Hitler?” You said, appalled. “And you’re the millions he killed.” “I’m Jesus?” “And you’re everyone who followed him.” You fell silent. “Every time you victimized someone,” I said, “you were victimizing yourself. Every act of kindness you’ve done, you’ve done to yourself. Every happy and sad moment ever experienced by any human was, or will be, experienced by you.” You thought for a long time. “Why?” You asked me. “Why do all this?” “Because someday, you will become like me. Because that’s what you are. You’re one of my kind. You’re my child.” “Whoa,” you said, incredulous. “You mean I’m a god?” “No. Not yet. You’re a fetus. You’re still growing. Once you’ve lived every human life throughout all time, you will have grown enough to be born.” “So the whole universe,” you said, “it’s just…” “An egg.” I answered. “Now it’s time for you to move on to your next life.” And I sent you on your way.

Welcome to Voat! If you don't mind me asking, do you know or have any experience in cybersecurity? I'm really wanting to get a job in it in the upcoming months.

Also, narcolepsy? Don't feel too bad or out of place. I actually suffer from adult ADD. I tend to "space out" and lose focus on what I'm doing sometimes, especially when I have a lot of thoughts running through my mind.

Network security was my major when I first went to college, actually. I'll be perfectly honest, though, I don't get to do enough of it to call myself a professional in that particular area. However, I know a few guys in the field and speak with them regularly.

Now, I'm not sure of your background so pardon me if anything I say is redundant for you. First, always keep your certs up. It shows you're serious about the networking field. The Cisco security cert is pretty expensive to obtain but if you can get a job to pay for it, that's ace.

Second, it's far easier to transfer into cyber security than getting a job outright. Don't get me wrong, there are entry level netsec jobs out there (look for the assistant positions). For instance, recently Delta was looking for people to fill Assistant Security Technicians. The job was contract and it basically had you working alongside a senior Security Tech. In addition, some tech jobs these days will help pay for your certs or pay for them outright. Like in school if you took the Cisco course, you'd get a voucher for the cert test. Same thing. You can usually maneuver this to your advantage by obtaining certs that are otherwise a bit too expensive to obtain on your own. I did this with a terrible IT outsourcing company I worked for in order to obtain cheaper certs and pay some bills. You can then use your new certs to apply and bargain for a netsec job in your company. It will show dedication and a willingness to advance.

Third, read. Seriously. If you want to be a boss at netsec, it's very important to keep your eye on the latest networking sites/blogs/subverses/etc. Learning about attacks before they can occur will help prevent disasters. Netsec is rarely a passive job when taken seriously. Granted, you can say that about most jobs, but most of my netsec friends ended up being more like researchers than techs. They reproduce things in their home which they read on the Internet and applied it to their knowledge base. They poke and prod on test servers just to see if it's possible to break it from the outside. They are curious people by nature. Then again, so are hackers so I suppose it's a match made in heaven.

Again, I don't know where you are in your career. Maybe you've already gotten your Cisco security cert. Maybe you have a few years experience to help guide you through complicated systems to accomplish singular tasks. Maybe you have a home server that you continually attempt to break into. I don't know. But that's as much as I know about the industry atm.

Ooo! Also, network. Like, with people. Sometimes these jobs are easier to get into if you know someone in the industry or a netsec friend is leaving their job and can recommend someone to their boss. Going to stuff like DEFCON can be a real great way to make connections as well. I'd say go to it anyway. Last time I went I had a ton of fun.

Thanks for the info!

Ah, I see. Well, I always saw netsec/cybersec as sort of a specialization within networking. If you want to do anything with networks, it's great to have field knowledge of the concepts. I can't overstate that enough. I have to Google stuff now and then when I run across a weird command or situation in *nix. My security buddies are the guys I go to if I can't find what I want through the forums and Google. These are the guys that seem to know very specific stuff. Their level of knowledge is better than mine. If you really want to gun for one of the more serious security jobs, it's going to probably require a lot of other expertise. Even physical security comes into play as these guys have a hand in designing it sometimes.

Also, it's good to check out the types of security jobs (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_security#The_cyber_security_job_market). While it is Wikipedia and these aren't all the security related jobs, it does get the point across. Different companies will offer different positions in varying amounts of openings. For instance, offensive cyberwarfare specialists will typically be found among US alphabet agencies like FBI, NSA, CIA, DHS, and etc. I know it's not a popular opinion these days but those guys really do know more about the Internet and networks than most and it's the logical conclusion for many netsec professionals. In addition, private security firms (Mitnick Security Consulting, LLC) are a great place if you can gain employment for one. I don't personally know anyone in the private sector but I hear the pay is very good but gaining access is harder. Many people prefer to go the Federal route and then move to the private sector. Federal training + military background = perfect private sector material. If I were you, I'd probably go for that route. It's a long-term investment but if that's what you want, then you have a good chance of getting it that way.

College-wise, you may wish to try for a dual major like I did. Network Administration and Security. Network Engineering and Security. There are a couple of different combos you can go with depending on what you want. The point is that the Security major will get you the specialized knowledge required to get hired into these jobs. The Admin/Engineering major provides the framework necessary to reach the higher levels of your specialization in security. Also, college courses will provide vouchers as I previously mentioned. Grab your Cisco certs, grab your Net+ certs, A+ should be an easy pass for you, and any engineering certs would be good too. There's also a few IT management certs you could pick up along the way to increase your overall value. Just remember not to overdue it. Jack-of-All-Trades syndrome is actually why I can't find a job at the moment. My field experience covers such a large breadth that I can't be hired for the specific roles I want. Ooo! Also, some colleges will provide job placement in the area of your major but that was 2006 when I was in college, so things may have changed a little.

Final notes? Know *nix like the back of your hand. Red Hat, Debian, Arch, Ubuntu, Slackware, Kali (super important for pen-testing). The less you have to Google, the more successful you will be. I guarantee it. And always remember, there is always something to learn. There is always something to find. There is always a way to break something.
